Friday: Bidisha's reply to Mehak's long message about the weekend was just "ok." Mehak stared at it in the college canteen until her tea went cold. By evening she had sent, "If you're done with me, just say it."
Saturday: Bidisha called, confused. She had been stuck in a lab all day. Mehak's face burned. "I don't know why I said that," she muttered, and spent most of the afternoon under her quilt, sick with shame.
Two weeks later: another short "ok" arrived. Mehak felt the same drop in her stomach, and this time she noticed it. She wrote, "Small panic here, not your fault. Are we still on for Sunday?" Bidisha sent back, "Of course. Lab again. Sunday, samosas, you and me."

qa.q: What did Bidisha's first reply say?
qa.a: It was just "ok."

qa.q: What did Mehak feel on Saturday after Bidisha's call, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed; her face burned and she spent most of the afternoon under her quilt.

qa.q: What changed the second time a short reply arrived?
qa.a: Mehak noticed the drop in her stomach, named it as a small panic, and asked a simple question instead of lashing out.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt receiving "If you're done with me, just say it" after a long day in the lab?
qa.a: She was confused and probably hurt, since she had done nothing except be busy.

grounding: A young woman reads a short reply as rejection, lashes out and feels shame, then later notices her fear and asks for reassurance calmly.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: Ojas, beta, sit. Your Anand chacha was not always this calm, you know. At twenty-one I was in love with your chachi, and I was a mess. If she spoke to another boy in class, I'd go silent for days. If she was ten minutes late to the bus stand, I'd think, that's it, she's leaving. Once I shouted at her in front of the college gate for laughing at someone else's joke. Afterwards I couldn't look at her, I felt so small. She didn't leave. She sat me down and said, "I'm not going anywhere, but you can't shout at me." Slowly I started telling her, "I'm scared," instead of getting angry. Forty years married now. Still scared sometimes. I just say so.

qa.q: Where did Anand once shout at the woman he loved?
qa.a: He shouted at her in front of the college gate.

qa.q: How did Anand feel after shouting, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt ashamed; he couldn't look at her and felt very small.

qa.q: What turning point helped Anand change?
qa.a: She told him she wasn't leaving but that he couldn't shout at her, and he began saying "I'm scared" instead of getting angry.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Ojas's chachi when Anand went silent for days?
qa.a: She was likely confused and hurt, punished for ordinary things like talking in class or running late.

grounding: An uncle recalls reading small cues as rejection at twenty-one, lashing out, feeling shame and slowly softening with a steady partner.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: Sit, beta, since you asked why your Dada and I still hold hands. At twenty I was a nightmare to love. If Chetan came to the college gate five minutes late, I decided he was bored of me. If he laughed with a classmate, I went silent for two days, then burst out with cruel things, then cried in the hostel bathroom, ashamed. Once I threw his letters back at him in the library. He didn't shout. He picked them up and said, "Damini, I'm not going anywhere. But you must tell me when you're scared, not punish me." That was my turning point. I began saying, "I'm frightened you'll leave," out loud. It sounded foolish. It worked, slowly, over years.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: Irfan's train to Kolkata ran through the night, twenty hours, most of it without network. He had warned her. Still, when his good-night message didn't come, Reena lay awake rereading his last text, "ok ttyl". He usually wrote more. By two in the morning she had sent six messages, the last one: "Fine, just say you're done with me." In the morning they all showed as read at once, and his reply came: "Reena?? No signal for hours. What happened?" Her face burned. She typed and deleted three excuses. Then she wrote the truth: "I got scared you were leaving. I'm sorry about that last message. I'm working on it." He called from the next station.

qa.q: How many messages had Reena sent by two in the morning?
qa.a: Six messages.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when Irfan's reply came?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, her face burning, after reading a short text and silence as rejection.

qa.q: Which choice helped repair things, and why?
qa.a: Writing the truth about being scared instead of an excuse, because it let Irfan understand and respond warmly.

qa.q: What is it like for Irfan to wake up to six messages?
qa.a: He is probably confused and worried, since he had warned her about the network and did nothing wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who reads a short text and silence as rejection, lashes out and feels shame, then names the fear.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: At Zubin's cousin's engagement in Bandra, he spent ten minutes on the balcony talking to an old college friend, and Zeenat felt the whole evening tilt. She stood by the snacks, smiling stiffly, counting. When he came back she said, too loudly, "Go on, she's more interesting." Two aunties turned. In the taxi she stared out at the dark sea, cheeks hot, wanting to disappear. Zubin was quiet a while, then said, "That hurt. But I think you got scared." She nodded, eyes stinging. "You talk to anyone for ten minutes and my brain says you're leaving." He took her hand. That week she began writing down each time it happened, and what had actually been true.

qa.q: How long did Zubin talk to the old college friend?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling in the taxi?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and embarrassed, cheeks hot, knowing her fear of being left had made her lash out.

qa.q: What small step did Zeenat take afterwards?
qa.a: She started writing down each time the fear came and what had actually been true, to build self-awareness.

qa.q: How does Zubin respond to Zeenat's outburst?
qa.a: He admits it hurt but sees the fear under it and takes her hand, which makes it safer for her to be honest.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a small cue as rejection, lashing out, feeling shame, then softening with self-awareness and a safe partner.

passage:
"You said 'fine' with a full stop," Arohi said, standing in the doorway of the flat. "That means you're annoyed with me."
Francis looked up from the laptop. "It means I'm finishing a report."
"You always do this. You pull away and then you'll just leave one day."
"Arohi—"
"Forget it!" She slammed the bedroom door.
Twenty minutes later she opened it, eyes red. "I'm sorry. That was horrible of me."
"It was a lot," Francis said quietly. "What happened?"
"When you went short, I felt like you were already gone. It's an old fear. It isn't about the full stop."
"Thank you for telling me. I'm not going anywhere. Next time, can you ask me first, before the door?"
Arohi nodded, ashamed and a little relieved. "I'll try. Ask first."

qa.q: What was Francis doing when Arohi came to the doorway?
qa.a: Francis was finishing a report on the laptop.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel after slamming the door?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, calling it horrible, and also a little relieved once she explained her fear of being left.

qa.q: What did Francis ask Arohi to try next time?
qa.a: To ask first, before slamming the door, so the fear can be checked instead of acted on.

qa.q: How might Francis feel when Arohi says "you'll just leave one day"?
qa.a: Francis may feel hurt and accused over a report and a full stop, yet stays calm and reassures her once she explains.

grounding: Shows a young adult who reads a short reply as rejection, lashes out, then feels shame and names her fear of being left.
